mcqs.question: Why should already-deployed images be re-scanned periodically, not just once at build time?
options: Re-scanning is only needed if the image itself changes
New CVEs are discovered continuously, so a clean scan today doesn't guarantee the image stays clean tomorrow
Scanners become less accurate over time and need recalibration
It's not actually necessary — a build-time scan is sufficient forever
mcqs.explanation: Vulnerability databases grow constantly as new CVEs are discovered in existing packages — an image that passed scanning last month can have a newly discovered vulnerability today, even though its own content hasn't changed. Periodic re-scanning is what catches that.

mcqs.question: Which of these is NOT one of the three concrete least-privilege levers for hardening a container?
mcqs.explanation: Memory limits are a resource-control concern (cgroups), not a least-privilege one. The three levers that shrink blast radius if a container is compromised are non-root, read-only filesystem, and dropped capabilities.

mcqs.question: A team pulls a widely-used public base image with millions of downloads and ships it to production without scanning it. What's the flaw in this reasoning?
options: Popularity is actually a reliable proxy for current security — this is fine
Popularity says nothing about whether today's specific version has an unpatched CVE, and it doesn't protect against future upstream compromise
Public images can never be used in production regardless of scanning
Scanning is only useful for private, custom-built images
mcqs.explanation: Download count reflects adoption, not current vulnerability status — CVEs are discovered continuously and a maintainer account could be compromised at any time. Scanning is what actually verifies a specific image version's security posture, regardless of its popularity.
